title: The Male Greeting Taxonomy
hook: A greeting between men is a quick negotiation of distance, rank and history, settled in about two seconds by a nod, a grip, a pull or a hug.
why:
Men greet each other dozens of times a week, and almost none of it is taught. A boy learns, by watching and by getting it wrong, when to nod, when to shake hands, when a fist is offered and when arms are opening. By adulthood the choices happen so fast that most men could not say how they made them. Yet a greeting says a great deal: how close two people are, who holds the higher status, how long it has been, and whether anything has changed between them.

This chapter slows the greeting down. It describes the phases that greetings pass through, the ladder of options men use from a nod across a room to a full embrace, how to read the offer coming toward you and match it, how rank and setting change the rules, how greetings carry history and belonging, and what greetings seem to do that nobody notices. The handshake itself, and how it has changed since the pandemic, has its own chapter in Part IV; this one maps the whole territory around it.

teach.p:
In 1973 the anthropologist Adam Kendon and the psychiatrist Andrew Ferber filmed people arriving at a garden party and described what happened when they greeted one another. A full greeting, they found, passes through a sequence of phases. First comes sighting and the decision to approach. Then a distance salutation: a wave, a nod, a toss of the head, a smile, a raised hand or a call of hello, usually returned in kind. Often a small dip of the head follows, made by the person who will travel further.

During the approach itself, people usually look away from each other, glancing back only now and then, and many touch their hair or clothes. Then, in the final approach, the gaze returns, and the greeting ends in a close salutation: a handshake, an embrace, a kiss, or simply a nod and a few words at conversational distance.

Not every greeting includes every phase. Two colleagues passing in a corridor may stop at the distance salutation; old friends meeting at a station may run through every phase in a few seconds. But the sequence explains several things that otherwise look odd. The man walking toward you who suddenly looks at his feet is not avoiding you; he is in the approach phase, where looking away is normal. The awkward moment when you have greeted someone from too far away and still have ten metres to walk is a distance salutation with nowhere to go.

The figure here raises a hand in acknowledgement across a space. It is the distance salutation in its simplest form, and whether it is returned decides whether the rest of the greeting happens at all.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if greetings showed no regular sequence, or if mutual gaze were usual throughout the approach. Kendon's description has been widely used since, including by engineers designing greeting robots, but it was based on filmed observation of a limited range of settings.

teach.p:
Men have a set of greetings that can be arranged roughly from least to most contact. At the bottom is the nod across a room, up or down, which the next chapter takes apart. Next comes the raised hand or wave, then words alone at a distance. Then the first contact: a fist bump, knuckles meeting briefly with no grip. Then the handshake. Then the handshake pulled into a half embrace, with a slap on the back. Then the side hug, an arm across the shoulders. At the top is the full embrace.

Each rung claims more closeness than the one below. Choosing a rung is a statement about the relationship, and the other man reads it as one. Offering a handshake to a friend you usually hug can feel cold; offering a hug to a colleague you usually nod to can feel presumptuous. The rung also depends on the setting. The same two men might fist-bump at the gym, shake hands at a wedding and embrace at a funeral.

Time apart moves greetings up the ladder. The sociologist Erving Goffman, who called greetings and farewells access rituals, observed that they tend to grow warmer the longer people have been apart: friends who see each other daily may barely greet at all, while the same friends meeting after a year abroad may embrace.

Audience matters too. Many men greet each other more warmly in private than in front of colleagues, or more warmly among friends than in front of their fathers. The figures here meet at the lower rungs, knuckles touching. It is a greeting that asks for very little and offers a little more than a nod, which is exactly why it is popular.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men chose greetings without regard to relationship, setting or time apart. Observation and common experience strongly support the ladder, but the exact order of rungs varies between places, generations and groups.

teach.p:
A greeting is negotiated in motion, and the negotiation is mostly settled before anyone touches. As someone approaches, their hand tells you what they are offering. A hand coming forward low and to the side, thumb up and fingers together, is a handshake. A hand raised higher, thumb hooked, ready to clasp, is the start of a pull-in. A closed fist held out at chest height is a bump. Arms opening from the sides and a step that keeps coming is a hug. Hands that stay down, with a nod and a smile, are saying that words will do.

The safest rule is to match the offer. If a man extends his hand, shake it, even if you usually hug your friends. If he opens his arms and you are comfortable, accept the hug; if you are not, a warm two-handed handshake or a hand on his arm can honour the offer while keeping your distance.

If you want more closeness than the offer suggests, go one rung up and leave room for the other man to stay where he is: shake his hand and let a slight pull show that you would welcome a half embrace, without forcing it. If he resists the pull, let it go.

Collisions happen: one man offers a hand while the other goes in for a hug, and they end up in a tangle of elbows. The cure is to laugh, name it and try again: “Let's try that again.” Most awkward greetings are forgotten in seconds when someone acknowledges them lightly. The figures here shake hands in profile, arms meeting midway. Neither had to guess; each saw the other's hand coming and met it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if greetings could not be predicted from the approaching hand. Most people can tell what is coming in the last metre, but signals are sometimes ambiguous, which is why collisions happen and why matching sometimes fails.
teach.pullQuote: Match the offer coming toward you before adding anything of your own.

teach.h: Rank, setting and who goes first.
teach.p:
Greetings also say who is in charge. Kendon noticed that the person who moves further toward the other often makes the small dip of the head, a gesture of deference. Hosts usually move toward guests. Junior people often wait for senior ones to set the level of the greeting: whether it will be a handshake, a hug or a nod.

The chapter on touch described Nancy Henley's observation that touch tends to flow down hierarchies. Greetings follow the same rule. A manager who hugs a junior colleague, a coach who wraps an arm around a young player, an older man who claps a younger one on the back, are using a freedom the other person may not feel able to refuse. Where you hold power, let the person with less of it set the closeness. Offer a handshake or a nod, and go further only if they do.

Groups add their own rules. When a man joins a circle, he is expected to greet each member, usually in an order that follows seniority, closeness or simply position. Skipping one person, or giving him a lesser greeting than the others, is noticed by everyone, and is often meant to be. If you arrive at a group late and cannot greet everyone individually, a single greeting to the whole circle avoids singling anyone out.

Setting matters as much as rank. A greeting appropriate at a stag weekend can be wrong at a job interview, and the reverse. The figures here stand in a loose circle of three. Whoever joins next will have to decide, in a second or two, how to greet each of them, and the group will read every choice.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if greetings between people of unequal status were as freely refused as greetings between equals. Henley's pattern has been found to be weaker and more variable than she proposed, but the difficulty of refusing a powerful person's greeting is widely reported.

teach.p:
A greeting is also a short summary of a relationship. Two men who were close and have fallen out will often show it first in the greeting: a nod where there used to be a hug, a handshake that is brief and loose. A greeting withheld altogether, a man who looks through you, says more than any words.

Greetings can also carry the history of a group. Teammates, bands and old friends build elaborate handshakes of their own, sequences of grips, slaps and bumps that nobody else knows. Doing it is a way of saying we belong together. The best-known example in men's greetings is the dap, a sequence of slaps, grips and bumps that took shape among Black American soldiers in the late 1960s, during the Vietnam War. Accounts agree that it expressed solidarity and a promise to look out for one another in an army where they faced racism, and that some officers tried to ban it. Veterans carried it home, and it spread into wider culture. Its exact origins, and the claim that the name stands for dignity and pride, are disputed.

That history is a reason for care. A greeting that belongs to a group means something to its members, and copying it to seem friendly can land as mockery. Use the greetings people offer you, and learn a group's own greeting when you are invited to.

The figures here meet in a handshake pulled into a half embrace, hands still clasped between their chests. Between two friends, the strength of the pull and the number of slaps on the back are their own private dialect.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if greetings stayed the same whatever had happened between two people. The claim rests on observation and experience rather than measurement, and the history of the dap rests on accounts that differ in their details.

teach.h: Greetings do more than you know.
teach.p:
Greetings may also be doing things that nobody notices. In 2015 Idan Frumin, Noam Sobel and their colleagues secretly filmed 271 people who were greeted by an experimenter, some with a handshake and some without. After shaking hands with an experimenter of the same gender, people more than doubled the time they spent with their own right hand near their nose, the hand that had done the shaking. After shaking hands with someone of the other gender, it was the left hand that rose to the face more often.

The researchers suggested that handshakes may serve, in part, to sample another person's scent, as many other mammals do when they meet. The people in the study had no idea they were doing it. The finding has not been widely repeated, and its interpretation is open, but it is a useful reminder that a greeting is a physical exchange as well as a symbolic one.

It also explains why greetings matter so much to how a meeting feels. A greeting sets the first impression of warmth, regard and physical comfort, before a word of substance has been said. A limp greeting, a distracted one made while looking at a phone, or one aimed past you at someone more important, can colour the next hour.

The figure here touches his face, an unremarkable gesture. In the minute after a handshake, it may not be quite as unremarkable as it looks. You do not need to watch for it. You only need to remember that greetings work on several levels at once.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people did not change how they touched their faces after a handshake. Frumin and colleagues found that they did, but in a single set of studies, and whether the purpose is scent is an interpretation rather than a proven fact.

teach.p:
The male greeting repertoire changes as soon as you cross a border. In parts of southern Europe, the Middle East and Latin America, men who know each other may kiss on the cheek or embrace as a matter of course. In Japan, a bow may replace any touch. In Thailand, the wai, palms pressed together, does the work of the handshake. In many Muslim communities, a hand placed on the heart accompanies or replaces a handshake, especially between men and women. The chapter on cultural calibration in Part VI described how to learn a local pattern, and Part V offers a working map.

Within any culture, families, regions and generations differ. Younger men in many countries greet each other with more physical contact than their fathers did. Many men who grew up without hugs have learned to give them, and some have not.

Farewells deserve the same attention as greetings. Goffman noted that the two mirror each other, bracketing the time together. A parting is often warmer than the arrival, because the time together has done its work: men who shook hands on arrival may embrace on leaving. A cold farewell after a warm greeting tells you that something happened in between.

The figure here places a hand on the heart. It is a greeting, a thank you and a farewell in many places, and a reminder that what counts as a proper greeting depends entirely on where you are and who you are with.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if male greetings were the same everywhere. They plainly are not, though descriptions of national patterns can exaggerate differences that are wide within each country as well.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Going in for a hug he did not offer
poseGallery.annotation: The safest greeting is the one that matches the offer coming toward you. If you want more closeness, go one rung up and let him choose.

poseGallery.doCaption: A raised hand from across the room
poseGallery.dontCaption: Arriving with your eyes on a phone
poseGallery.annotation: A greeting begins at a distance. A distracted arrival says that the person you are meeting is not your first concern.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Skipping one man in the circle
poseGallery.annotation: In a group, everyone notices who was greeted and how. If you cannot greet each person, greet the whole circle at once.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Pushing a handshake on a man who greets with palms together
poseGallery.annotation: Greetings change across cultures and faiths. Match the greeting offered, and the respect is understood without a word.

poseGallery.doCaption: A warm hello, leaving the level to them
poseGallery.dontCaption: A boss hugging a junior who cannot refuse
poseGallery.annotation: Touch flows down hierarchies. If you are senior, offer the lighter greeting, and let the other person choose whether to come closer.

caseStudy:
Danny, thirty-four, starts a new job as a site manager on a large building project. On his first morning he notices that every greeting on the site follows rules he does not yet know. The foreman, Pete, gives him an upward nod from across the yard and nothing more. The young labourers fist-bump each other and him. Tomasz, the senior carpenter, comes across, stops at a precise distance and holds out his hand, low and to the side, every morning without fail.

On the second day Danny, keen to fit in, offers Tomasz a fist. Tomasz looks at it, keeps his hand where it is, and Danny ends up bumping his knuckles against an open palm. Both laugh, but Danny notices that Tomasz is a little cooler for the rest of the day. The next morning he watches Tomasz's hand as he approaches, and shakes it properly. Tomasz nods, satisfied.

Kwame, the electrician, shakes hands and finishes with a snap of the fingers that he grew up with in Ghana. Danny gets it wrong twice. On the third attempt he asks Kwame to show him slowly, and Kwame, delighted, teaches him in front of the crew.

Danny also notices what he must not copy. Pete, the foreman, slaps the apprentices on the back as he greets them, and one of them, a quiet nineteen-year-old, stiffens every time. Danny, who has authority over all of them, keeps to handshakes and nods with the apprentices.

By the end of the month Danny greets six men six different ways each morning, without thinking. When Pete's father dies and he comes back to work after the funeral, Pete walks straight past the nod and shakes Danny's hand, holding it a moment longer than usual.
observe: Watch three greetings between men today, and pick out the phases: distance salutation, approach, close salutation.
Notice how your own greeting changes with different people: a close friend, a colleague, your boss, your father.
Before your next few greetings, watch the other person's hand as they approach, and notice what it tells you.
Notice a greeting that was withheld, downgraded or upgraded, and what it said about the relationship.

drills.name: Greeting Inventory
steps: List ten men you see regularly.
Beside each, write how you usually greet him and how he greets you.
Mark any greetings that do not match, where one of you offers more than the other.
Note any greetings that have changed over the years, and why.
Write one sentence about what the list says about your relationships.
variations: Do the inventory for women you see regularly, and compare the greetings with those you use with men.
Ask one man on your list how he would describe your greeting, and whether he would like it to change.

drills.name: Read the Hand
steps: For one week, before each greeting, predict from the other man's approach what he is about to offer.
Note the cues you used: hand height, fist or open hand, arms, pace.
At the end of the week, count your accuracy and the cues that worked best.
variations: Do the exercise at a busy event, such as a wedding or a match, where many greetings happen quickly.
Watch a sports broadcast before a match, and predict each greeting between players from their approach.

drills.name: One Rung Up
steps: Choose a friend you would like to be closer to.
Decide which rung of the greeting ladder you usually use with him, and which rung is one step up.
Next time you meet, offer the next rung lightly, leaving room for him to stay where he is.
Notice how he responds, and accept it either way.
Write down what happened and how it felt.
variations: Choose a friend you see less often than you would like, and offer one rung up at your next meeting.
Notice a greeting that someone else offered you one rung up, and how you responded.

drills.name: Recover a Collision
steps: With a willing friend, act out a greeting collision: one offers a hand, the other a hug.
Practise the recovery line, such as “Let's try that again,” said with a laugh.
Practise the reverse, so you can recover from either side.
Notice how quickly the awkwardness disappears when it is named.
variations: Practise recovering a cheek-kiss collision, which is common in many cultures, as well as a handshake and fist collision.
Practise the recovery line in a new setting, such as a work event, so that it comes naturally under mild pressure.

quiz.q: A man looks down at the ground as he walks toward you to say hello. What does Kendon's work on greetings suggest?
options: He is avoiding you and does not really want to say hello to you
Looking away during the approach is a normal part of greeting
He is nervous and is very likely hiding something from you
He has not recognised you yet and is unsure who you are
quiz.explain: Kendon and Ferber found that people usually avert their gaze during the approach phase and look back in the final approach. Reading it as avoidance mistakes a normal phase for a message.

quiz.q: What did Frumin and colleagues observe after people shook hands with someone of the same gender?
options: They washed their hands more often over the following ten minutes
They rated the other person as noticeably warmer and more trustworthy afterwards
They more than doubled the time spent with the shaking hand near the nose
They avoided touching their own faces for the rest of the visit
quiz.explain: In secretly filmed sessions, people more than doubled the time their shaking hand spent near their nose after a same-gender handshake. The researchers suggested handshakes may partly serve to sample scent, an interpretation still open to debate.

quiz.q: You usually fist-bump your friends. An older colleague walks toward you with his hand coming forward, low and to the side. What fits best?
options: Offer your fist anyway, so that he learns how you like to be greeted
Give him a quick nod and keep both of your hands by your sides
Go in for a half hug, so that he knows you consider him a friend
Shake his hand, matching the greeting he is already offering
quiz.explain: His hand is offering a handshake, and the safest rule is to match the offer. You can add warmth through the grip and your words without imposing your own style.

quiz.q: A manager wants to greet the junior members of his team warmly. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Let them set the level: offer a handshake or nod, go further only if they do
Hug everyone in exactly the same way, so that nobody on the team feels left out
Slap each of them on the back, since that is how men greet at work
Avoid greeting them at all, so that he cannot be misread by anyone
quiz.explain: Touch and greetings tend to flow down hierarchies, and a junior may not feel free to refuse. Letting the person with less power set the closeness keeps the greeting warm without pressure.

quiz.q: What does the history of the dap illustrate about greetings between men?
options: Greetings are purely functional and carry no other meaning
Elaborate greetings were first invented by marketing departments
A greeting can carry belonging and solidarity within a group
Military rules have always encouraged elaborate greetings
quiz.explain: The dap took shape among Black American soldiers as an expression of solidarity, and some officers tried to ban it. Greetings that belong to a group mean something to its members, which is why copying them uninvited can go wrong.

quiz.q: According to Goffman's observations, how does time apart usually affect a greeting between friends?
options: The longer the time apart, the more formal and distant the greeting
The longer the time apart, the warmer and fuller the greeting tends to be
Time apart makes no difference once two people are close friends
Long absences mean friends usually skip the greeting altogether
quiz.explain: Goffman noted that greetings tend to grow warmer the longer people have been apart. Friends who meet daily may barely greet, while the same friends may embrace after a year away.

quiz.q: In Kendon and Ferber's description, what usually comes soon after sighting, before people get close?
options: A distance salutation, such as a wave, a nod or a call of hello
A firm handshake given from several metres away across the room
A long, unbroken stare held throughout the whole of the approach
Nothing at all, since greetings only begin when people are close
quiz.explain: After sighting and the decision to approach, people usually make a distance salutation, such as a wave, nod or smile, often returned in kind. Looking away during the approach that follows is normal.

quiz.q: Your brother has always greeted you with a hug. Since an argument about your father's will, he nods at you from across the room and stays away. What fits this chapter best?
options: Nod back and keep your distance, since that is clearly what he wants
Ignore him for the rest of the day so he knows how hurtful the nod was
Treat the nod as a sign of the history, and find a private moment to talk
Walk over and hug him anyway, in front of everyone, to make the point
quiz.explain: A downgraded greeting is often the first visible sign that a relationship has shifted. Answering it in kind keeps the distance; a private word about the history behind it offers a way back.

quiz.q: Someone says that a crushing handshake shows confidence and is always respected. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since the strongest grip always makes the best impression
A firm, full grip helps first impressions in some research; crushing does not
It is right in business but wrong in social settings, where grip does not matter
It is wrong, since any physical contact in a greeting makes a bad impression
quiz.explain: Chaplin and colleagues linked firmer, fuller handshakes to more positive first impressions. But a painful grip reads as aggressive or insecure, and norms vary across cultures.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific man whose greeting with you has changed over the years, warmer or colder. Describe how you greeted each other at first, how you greet each other now, and what happened in between. Then think about one greeting in your life that does not match, where one of you offers more closeness than the other. What do you think each of you is saying, and is there anything you would like to change?
reflection.guidance: Greetings are small, so it is easy to dismiss them, but they often record the history of a relationship more honestly than words do. Describe the actual movements: the nod, the hand, the pull, the hug, the slaps. If you would like a greeting to change, the next drill offers a way to try one rung up without forcing it.

failureMode: The first failure is to impose your own greeting, offering a fist to a man who is holding out his hand, or charging into a hug he did not offer, rather than reading the offer coming toward you and matching it. The second is to ignore power: a senior man who hugs, back-slaps or embraces junior colleagues may be using a freedom they cannot refuse. The third is to read a normal phase as a message, such as treating the gaze aversion of the approach as avoidance. The fourth is to copy a group's greeting uninvited, so that it lands as mockery. And the fifth is to forget that greetings record relationships, so that a downgraded greeting, or a greeting withheld, goes unnoticed when it is the first sign that something has changed.

furtherStudy.note: Folklife magazine, 2014. A short history of the dap, from soldiers in Vietnam to everyday greeting.

moreCases.title: The hug at the reunion
moreCases.scene:
Gary, fifty, is at his school's thirty-year reunion in a hotel function room. Across the room he spots Neil, who was his best friend from the age of eleven until they fell out over a girl at nineteen and stopped speaking. Gary has thought about Neil many times since. He has had two pints, he is feeling sentimental, and he strides across the room with his arms already opening.

Neil sees him coming. He smiles, a little stiffly, and puts out his right hand, low and to the side, thumb up. His feet stop moving. Gary keeps coming, ignores the hand, and wraps Neil in a full hug, slapping his back twice. Neil's arms stay mostly at his sides; one hand pats Gary's shoulder once. When Gary lets go, Neil steps back half a pace, says "Good to see you, Gary," and, after a minute of small talk, says he must go and find someone.

Gary spends the rest of the evening feeling rejected, and tells another old friend that Neil is still holding a grudge after thirty years.

Gary had imagined this moment on the drive to the hotel: the two of them laughing, the years falling away. He had not imagined Neil's hand coming out first, and when it did, he simply did not see it.

Neil had come to the reunion half hoping to see Gary and half dreading it. He had decided in the car that a handshake would be the right way to start, and that if it went well, they might have a drink later.
moreCases.misread:
Gary read the moment through his own feelings: warmth, nostalgia and two pints. He did not read the offer coming towards him, a handshake and a stopped approach, and so he answered a question Neil had not asked.

And because he had acted on his own feelings rather than Neil's offer, he then read Neil's withdrawal as a grudge, when it was a reaction to the hug itself.

He also read his own sentimental warmth as shared, because the reunion felt to him like a happy occasion. For Neil, it was a cautious one.
moreCases.betterRead: A greeting is negotiated in motion, and the incoming offer tells you most of what you need to know. Neil's hand forward, low and to the side, and his feet stopping were a clear offer of a handshake, the right rung for two men who had not spoken in thirty years. Gary's hug claimed a closeness that the history did not yet support, and Neil's stiff arms and half-step back were the body withdrawing from a claim it had not agreed to. That was not necessarily a grudge. It may simply have been too much, too soon. The better reading was to match the offer: take the handshake, warmly, perhaps with the left hand briefly on Neil's arm, and say how good it was to see him. A greeting that starts at the right rung leaves room to climb. Later that evening, Gary went back, shook Neil's hand, apologised for the ambush and asked if they could have a drink sometime. Neil said he would like that. They met a month later, and at the end of the evening it was Neil who opened his arms.

moreCases.title: The manager who hugged everyone
moreCases.scene:
Steve, forty-five, joins a marketing agency as head of department. He is warm and energetic, and he believes in a close team. On his first morning he greets each of his twelve staff with a hug: a big, friendly embrace, sometimes with a slap on the back. He hugs them again at the end of every week, and on birthdays.

Most of the team go along with it. Some seem to enjoy it. But Sana, twenty-four, a junior designer, starts arriving at the office late enough to miss the Monday greetings, and Josh, twenty-two, the newest graduate, stiffens visibly each time, his arms barely moving. Neither says anything. Sana mentions it to a colleague, who says that Steve is just a hugger and means well, and that complaining would make her look difficult.

Steve thinks the team is warming up nicely. He has noticed that some people are a bit shy, and plans to help them come out of their shells.

Steve's previous company was a small start-up where everyone hugged, and he loved the culture there. He has brought it with him as a gift, without asking whether this team wants it.

Steve has also started greeting clients with hugs when they visit the office. Two of them have mentioned it to the account director, who has not yet decided whether to say anything.
moreCases.misread:
Steve read the team's going along with his hugs as acceptance, and Sana's and Josh's stiffness as shyness to be overcome. He did not consider that people junior to him might feel they could not refuse.

The colleague's advice, that complaining would make Sana look difficult, was itself a sign of how hard it is for junior staff to say no to a senior person's greeting.

And because the hugs were meant kindly, it did not occur to Steve that kindness can also be a pressure, when it comes from someone who decides your pay and your prospects.
moreCases.betterRead: The chapter on touch described Nancy Henley's observation that touch tends to flow down hierarchies, and greetings follow the same rule. A manager's hug is a greeting that junior staff cannot easily decline, which means that their going along with it says little about whether they want it. Sana's arriving late to avoid it and Josh's stiff arms were signs of discomfort being managed rather than voiced. The better approach for someone in Steve's position is to let junior people set the level of the greeting. A warm hello, a nod or a handshake, offered in a way that is easy to match, leaves them free to offer more if they want to. When a colleague who knew Sana well quietly mentioned the problem to Steve, he was mortified. He stopped hugging, switched to a warm hello and a handshake if one was offered, and told the team he had got it wrong. Sana started arriving on time again. A few months later, two of the team hugged him at the Christmas party, on their own initiative.

moreCases.title: The nod where the hug used to be
moreCases.scene:
Rob and his brother Stuart, both in their forties, have always greeted each other with a hug and a slap on the back, since they were teenagers. Six months ago their father died, and there has been a painful disagreement over the will. They have not discussed it directly; their wives have done most of the talking.

At their mother's seventieth birthday lunch, Stuart arrives late. He sees Rob across the room and gives him a short, upward nod. He does not walk over. When they end up next to each other at the buffet, Stuart says "All right?" and keeps his hands on his plate.

Rob feels it like a blow. Their mother, who has noticed nothing, asks why the two of them are not sitting together.

Rob's wife has noticed it too. She says quietly, as they help themselves to salad, that Stuart has not looked at Rob once since he arrived. Rob says he knows.

Rob has also noticed that Stuart arrived with a present for their mother that was clearly from both him and his wife, and that Stuart's wife, Claire, greeted Rob with her usual hug and an apologetic look. Whatever Stuart is feeling, Claire does not share it, or does not show it.

Later, when they all line up for a family photograph, Stuart stands at the far end, beside his mother, rather than next to Rob as he always has. Their mother tells them to squeeze together, and Stuart moves half a step and no further.
moreCases.misread:
Rob read the nod correctly as a downgrade, but his first instinct was to answer it with one of his own, and to spend the lunch on the other side of the room. A greeting withheld can easily become a greeting returned in kind.

Their mother's not noticing was also a reminder that greetings between adult brothers are often invisible to everyone except the brothers themselves.

He also nearly made the nod into a story about the whole relationship, when it was a story about one painful thing that had not been talked about.
moreCases.betterRead: Greetings carry history, and a change in a familiar greeting is often the first visible sign that something in the relationship has shifted. Stuart's nod in place of thirty years of hugs, and his hands staying on his plate at the buffet, were a message about the will that neither brother had yet put into words. Rob's reading was accurate. What mattered was what he did with it. Matching the downgrade would have kept the distance. The better response was to treat the greeting as information and find a private moment to respond to the history behind it. After lunch, Rob found Stuart in the garden and said, "We used to hug, and today you nodded. I don't want the will to cost us that. Can we talk about it properly, just the two of us?" Stuart was silent, then said he had felt pushed aside. They met for a drink the following week, without their wives, and talked for three hours. At Christmas, Stuart walked across the room and hugged him.

moreCases.title: The handshake with a snap
moreCases.scene:
Kofi, twenty-six, moves from Accra to Glasgow to start a graduate job at an engineering firm. On his first day, his line manager, Iain, holds out his hand. Kofi shakes it and, at the end, slides his middle finger against Iain's to make a quick snapping sound, as he would with a friend at home. Iain looks startled and pulls his hand back. Kofi laughs, then realises Iain is not laughing, and apologises.

Over the next week, Kofi notices that his greetings keep misfiring. He offers the snap handshake to a colleague, who looks confused. He greets an older woman in accounts with a slight bow and a two-handed handshake, as he would greet an elder at home, and she seems taken aback. He starts to feel that everything he does with his hands is wrong, and begins to greet people with only a nod.

His colleague Fiona, who has worked in West Africa, notices that the warmest person in the office has started to seem distant.

At home, Kofi's greetings were one of the things people liked most about him. His uncle used to say that you could tell how Kofi felt about someone by how he shook their hand.

In the second week, Kofi stops greeting the older woman in accounts at all, in case he gets it wrong again, and she, in turn, wonders whether she offended him.
moreCases.misread:
Iain read the snap as something odd or inappropriate, and Kofi, in turn, read the misfires as proof that his own greetings were wrong. Each side read the other through their own repertoire.

And because Iain pulled his hand back, Kofi read the startled reaction as disapproval of him, when it was only surprise at something unfamiliar.

Kofi's retreat into nods was also a misreading, of himself: he concluded that his way of greeting was wrong, when it was only unfamiliar. The longer he hid it, the less of himself his colleagues saw.

Iain's own surprise was understandable, and his pulling back was a reflex, not a judgment. Reflexes, though, are read as judgments by the person on the other end.
moreCases.betterRead:
The male greeting repertoire changes as soon as you cross a border. The finger snap at the end of a handshake is common between friends in Ghana, and a two-handed handshake with a slight bow is a mark of respect for elders in many West African cultures. Neither is odd; both are greetings in a different dialect. Kofi's retreat into nods was the cost of the misreadings: a warm man becoming distant because his warmth kept landing wrongly. The better approach, which Fiona helped with, was for both sides to learn a little of the other's dialect. She told Kofi what Glasgow handshakes usually look like, and told Iain, when he mentioned the snap, what it meant in Ghana. Iain, to his credit, asked Kofi to teach him. A month later the two of them had a handshake that ended with a snap, which Iain was very proud of, and Kofi had stopped nodding at everyone.

Fiona also told the office manager, who added a short note about greetings to the welcome pack for new international graduates, so that the next person would not have to work it out alone.

workedReading.title: Greeting a circle at a wedding
workedReading.scene:
Marcus, thirty-eight, arrives late at the evening reception of his cousin's wedding. Near the bar stands a circle of five men he knows to different degrees: his father-in-law, Clive, sixty-eight, whom he respects and finds slightly formal; his best friend, Jay; his cousin Tyler, twenty-four, the groom's brother; a man he has never met; and Dean, a former colleague he left a job because of, with whom things ended badly. As Marcus approaches, Jay sees him and his face lights up.

Marcus has been dreading seeing Dean. He knew Dean would be there, because Dean is a friend of the groom, and he has decided in advance that tonight is not the night to deal with it.

The reception is loud and crowded, and the circle is near the bar, where people keep pushing past. Whatever greetings Marcus makes, he will have to make them quickly, in a small space, with an audience.

steps.label: Make the distance salutation
steps.text:
From across the room, Marcus raises a hand and smiles towards the group as a whole, and gets nods and smiles back. He lets his gaze drop slightly as he walks the last few metres, which Kendon and Ferber noted is a normal part of an approach, so that he does not arrive staring at anyone.

He also slows his pace slightly as he gets close, which gives everyone a moment to see him coming and prepare their own greeting.

He also notes who sees him first. Jay's face lighting up tells him that the circle will turn towards him, and that he has a few seconds to read each man's offer before he arrives.

steps.label: Read each offer
steps.text:
As he arrives, he reads the hands. Jay's arms are already opening: a hug. Tyler's fist is coming up at chest height: a bump. Clive's hand comes forward, low and to the side: a handshake. The stranger's hands stay by his sides, with a polite smile: a nod and a name. Dean's hands stay in his pockets, and his eyes move to his drink: no offer at all.

He also notices that the offers fit what he knows of each relationship, which reassures him. If Jay had offered a handshake, or Clive a hug, he would have wondered what had changed.

He also notices Clive's slight straightening as he approaches, which is how Clive always prepares to shake hands. It is a small, reliable baseline, and it makes the reading easy.

steps.label: Mind the order and the rank
steps.text:
Marcus greets Clive first, with a firm, unhurried handshake and "Good to see you, Clive," because he is the senior man in the circle and his father-in-law. Then Jay, who gets the full hug he offered, and Tyler, the fist bump. The order is not a rule anyone wrote down, but it shows respect for the setting and for Clive's place in it.

He also stands at a slight angle to the circle as he greets each man, rather than pushing into the middle of it, so that the group stays open for the others.

He also gives Clive a moment of eye contact longer than the others, which is part of how respect is shown in a greeting without any extra words.

steps.label: Include the stranger
steps.text:
He turns to the man he does not know, smiles, and says, "Hi, I'm Marcus, the groom's cousin." The man says his name is Ravi and offers his hand at the last moment, which Marcus takes. Leaving a stranger out of a circle greeting is one of the easiest ways to make someone feel invisible, and one of the easiest to avoid.

He also remembers Ravi's name, and uses it later in the evening, which takes almost no effort and makes a stranger feel like a guest rather than a bystander.

He also keeps the introduction short and gives Ravi something to hold onto: who he is and how he fits in. A stranger in a circle of people who know each other often feels exposed, and a name and a connection help.

He also notes that Ravi's late hand came only after Marcus had introduced himself. Some people wait to see what a stranger offers before committing; matching their caution is part of reading them.

steps.label: Handle the hard one
steps.text:
With Dean, Marcus reads the hands in pockets and the eyes on the drink as a man who does not want a greeting beyond the minimum. He matches it: a short nod and "Dean," said evenly. He does not offer a hand that would be refused, or make a show of ignoring him. The history is there, and a wedding is not the place for it.

He also keeps his voice and face neutral rather than cold. A neutral greeting respects the history without escalating it, and leaves the door open for a better conversation another time.

He also keeps his body angled so that he is not facing Dean directly, and returns his attention to the others quickly. A brief, even acknowledgement and then moving on is often the kindest way through an awkward greeting.

He also makes a mental note to talk to Jay later about Dean, away from the circle, so that the history has somewhere to go that is not the middle of a wedding.

steps.label: Recover the collision
steps.text:
A few minutes later, Tyler goes to introduce Marcus to his girlfriend, and Marcus offers a hand just as she leans in for a cheek kiss. They bump awkwardly. Marcus laughs and says, "Let's try that again," and they do, with the kiss, and everyone laughs. Naming the collision lightly is the quickest way out of it.

He also notes that the girlfriend leaned in first, which told him what she expected. He simply had not read it fast enough, and the laugh repaired it.

He also lets the girlfriend lead the second attempt, so that the greeting happens on her terms, which is how most collisions are best repaired.

steps.label: Mark the parting
steps.text:
When Marcus leaves the circle to find his aunt, he does it properly: a hand on Jay's shoulder, a nod to Tyler, "See you later" to Ravi and Clive, and a brief nod to Dean. Partings mark relationships as much as greetings do, and leaving without one can read as a slight. Later, Clive tells Marcus's wife that Marcus has lovely manners, which Marcus finds slightly mortifying and secretly pleased about.

He also notes that his nod to Dean at parting was slightly warmer than the one at arrival. Dean nodded back, a little warmer too, which was more than Marcus had expected.

He also says a proper goodbye to Clive at the end of the night, with a handshake and a thank-you for the speech Clive gave. The parting is warmer than the greeting, which is how a good evening usually shows itself.

moreFailures.title: Imposing your own greeting
moreFailures.body:
The commonest greeting failure is to decide in advance what you will do and do it regardless of what the other person is offering: a fist to a man holding out his hand, a hug to a man who has stopped and extended his arm, a handshake to someone who greets with palms together. Each of these overrides the other person's offer, and the collision that follows is awkward at best and, at worst, a small act of disrespect. Watch the incoming hand, the arms and the pace of the approach, and match what is offered. If you want to offer more, offer it lightly, one rung up, and be ready to step back down if it is not returned.

It also helps to remember that people with injuries, arthritis or sensory sensitivities may avoid certain greetings for reasons that have nothing to do with you. A man who offers a fist or a nod instead of a handshake may be protecting a sore hand.

It also helps to notice your own habitual greeting and how it lands. A man who fist-bumps everyone may find that older men, women and people from other cultures experience it as overfamiliar; a man who shakes hands with everyone may seem stiff to younger friends.

When you are unsure what is coming, a slight pause with your hand ready, rather than committing early to a fist or a hug, gives the other person a moment to show their offer. A greeting that waits half a second rarely collides.

moreFailures.title: Ignoring power
moreFailures.body:
Greetings follow hierarchies, and the person with more power has more freedom to set the level. A manager who hugs his staff, a coach who wraps an arm round his players, an older relative who insists on kisses: each may mean warmth, and each is using a freedom that the other person cannot easily refuse. People lower in a hierarchy often go along with greetings they would rather avoid, which makes their compliance a poor guide to their wishes. If you are senior, offer the lighter rung, a warm hello, a nod or a handshake, and let the other person decide whether to move closer.

The same applies in families. An uncle who insists on hugging nieces and nephews who stiffen is using an elder's privilege. Children and young people should be allowed to choose a wave or a high five instead.

If you are junior and a greeting from someone senior makes you uncomfortable, it is reasonable to step slightly back and offer a handshake instead, or to mention it to someone you trust. You should not have to arrive late to avoid it.

It also helps to watch for the signs of a greeting being endured rather than enjoyed: arms that stay down during a hug, a body that turns slightly sideways, a quick step back afterwards. Those signs are worth taking seriously, especially from people junior to you.

moreFailures.title: Reading a normal phase as a message
moreFailures.body:
Many people misread the ordinary phases of a greeting. Kendon and Ferber found that people often look away or down during the approach, before the close salutation. That is a normal part of the sequence, not a sign of shyness, guilt or dislike. The same goes for the small dip of the head made by the person who travels further, which is a courtesy rather than submission, and for the brief pause before a handshake while two people judge the distance. Read the greeting as a whole, and against the person's baseline, before you decide that any single part of it means something.

It also helps to remember that some people avoid eye contact during greetings for reasons of culture, neurodivergence or shyness. A greeting with little eye contact can still be warm.

It also helps to remember that a greeting is short and noisy, and that most of the information in it is uncertain. A slightly weak handshake on one occasion means very little; a change that persists over weeks means more.

It also helps to separate the greeting from the person's mood that day. A brief, distracted handshake from a friend who has just had bad news says nothing about the friendship.

moreFailures.title: Skipping people and partings
moreFailures.body:
In a group, it is easy to greet the people you know best and overlook the rest: the quiet colleague, the partner of a friend, the stranger in the circle. Each one notices. The same applies to leaving. A man who slips away from a group without a word, or says goodbye to his friend and not to the people his friend was with, can leave behind an impression of coldness he did not intend. Greet each person in a small group, even briefly, and mark your exit. These are small courtesies with large effects.

At work, it helps to greet the cleaner, the receptionist and the security guard as you would greet a colleague. How someone greets people with less status says a great deal about them, and people notice.

It also helps to greet people who are often overlooked in groups: the new partner, the quiet child, the person in a wheelchair at a lower height, who is often greeted last or not at all.

And when someone arrives late to a group you are in, a quick greeting, even just eye contact and a nod, tells them they have been seen. Being ignored on arrival is one of the most common small hurts in group life.

questions.q: Why do people look away as they walk towards you to say hello?
questions.a:
It is a normal part of the greeting sequence. Kendon and Ferber found that after the distance salutation, a wave, nod or smile, people often look away or down during the approach, then look up again for the close greeting. Holding eye contact for the whole of a long approach would feel intense, even confrontational, and looking away gives both people a moment of privacy while they close the distance. It is not a sign that the person is shy, guilty or unfriendly. If someone looks down as they approach and then meets your eyes warmly at the handshake, the greeting has gone exactly as most greetings do.

It also helps to know that very long approaches, such as walking the length of a hall towards someone, are often awkward for everyone. A distance salutation early on, followed by looking away until you are close, is how most people manage them.

It also helps to know where to look when you are approaching. Glancing at the person, then at the floor or the space beside them, then back as you arrive, is the natural rhythm, and it avoids the stare that makes long approaches uncomfortable.

It also helps to know that some people find greetings themselves stressful, especially autistic people and people with social anxiety. A predictable, simple greeting, the same each time, can make it easier for them.

questions.q: Does a firm handshake really matter?
questions.a:
It can matter for first impressions. William Chaplin and colleagues found that people with firmer, fuller handshakes, with good eye contact, tended to make more positive first impressions, and that handshake quality was linked to perceived extraversion. But firm does not mean crushing. A grip that hurts reads as aggressive or insecure, and many people with arthritis or hand injuries find strong handshakes painful. Handshake norms also vary across cultures; in some, a softer, longer handshake is polite. Aim for a full, firm, brief grip, matched to the other person's, rather than a test of strength.

It also helps to match the other person's grip rather than impose your own. A firm grip offered to someone who gives a gentle one can feel like a contest; meeting them where they are feels like respect.

It may also help to dry your hands before an important handshake, if you know they get sweaty. It is a small, practical step that removes one source of worry.

And if someone offers a limp or brief handshake, do not read too much into it. Some people simply shake hands that way, and in some cultures a softer grip is the polite one.

questions.q: What should I do when a greeting goes wrong?
questions.a:
Name it lightly and try again. Collisions are common: a hand meeting a fist, a handshake meeting a hug, two people leaning the same way for a cheek kiss. Most people feel a jolt of embarrassment, and the quickest way through it is to laugh and say something like "Let's try that again" or "I never know which way to go." Then follow the other person's lead. Named with good humour, a collision becomes a small shared joke rather than an awkward moment, and it is usually forgotten within a minute. Pretending it did not happen tends to make it linger.

It also helps to remember that the other person feels the jolt too. Taking the lead in naming it, kindly, is a small generosity that most people appreciate.

It also helps to have a default for uncertain moments. Many people find that a smile and a slightly raised hand, ready to become a handshake if one is offered, covers most situations gracefully.

questions.q: Should I start hugging my male friends?
questions.a:
If you would like to, and they seem open to it, you can offer, one rung at a time. Many men find hugs with close friends easier than they expect, especially at moments that matter: a wedding, a funeral, a long-awaited reunion. The chapter on the bro hug describes how men often make hugs feel safe, with back slaps, a side angle or a brief duration. Read your friend's offer as he approaches. If his arms open, match them. If his hand comes forward, take it, and perhaps add your other hand on his arm. Accept either response. A friendship does not need a hug to be close, and a hug offered and declined is not a rejection of the friendship.

It may also help to notice moments when a hug would be natural, such as a goodbye before a long absence, a congratulation or a condolence. Those are often the easiest moments to move up a rung for the first time.

It also helps to notice how other men in your circle greet each other. If your friends hug each other, a hug is probably welcome; if they never do, a strong handshake with a hand on the arm may be the warmest rung that feels natural.

questions.q: Have greetings changed since the pandemic?
questions.a:
In many places, yes, at least for a while. During the COVID-19 pandemic, handshakes were discouraged and many people switched to nods, waves, elbow bumps or hands on hearts. Some have kept those habits, and some people remain uncomfortable with close contact. The chapter on the handshake in a post-handshake world takes this up. For a reader, the lesson is the same as always: watch the incoming offer, and if you are not sure, offer the lighter greeting and let the other person decide. Asking, "Handshake, or are we still nodding?" is perfectly acceptable.

It may also help to carry a lighter default for strangers in settings such as hospitals or care homes, where people may be unwell or anxious about infection.

It also helps to remember that people who are immunocompromised, elderly or caring for someone vulnerable may still prefer to avoid close contact. A greeting that respects that is a kindness, not an inconvenience.

Some workplaces settled on a new default during the pandemic, such as a nod or a wave, and kept it. Following the local custom is usually the safest choice when you are new.

questions.q: Why does how we say goodbye matter?
questions.a:
Because partings, like greetings, mark relationships. Goffman observed that greetings and farewells bracket encounters, acknowledging the relationship as people come together and part, and that a warmer farewell often reflects a longer separation ahead. Leaving without a goodbye can read as coldness, anger or indifference. A farewell that is warmer than the greeting can show that the time together went well. In families and close friendships, how people part, especially before a long absence, is often remembered. Mark your partings, even briefly, with the people who matter to you.

It also helps to notice the partings in your own life that were never properly made: friends who moved away without a goodbye, colleagues who left on a Friday without a word. Sometimes a message, even late, can mark what the parting did not.

It also helps to notice how children learn goodbyes. A father who always says goodbye properly, even when he is leaving for a few hours, teaches his children that partings matter.

It also helps to make farewells honest. "See you soon" from someone who means it, said with a hand on the shoulder, lands very differently from the same words thrown over a shoulder on the way out.

It also helps to say goodbye to the person who is staying as well as the person who is leaving. At the end of a visit, the host is often the one who is forgotten.

watch.title: Key & Peele: Obama Meet & Greet
watch.notice: A sketch in which the president changes his greeting for each person in a receiving line. Exaggerated, but every greeting in it is recognisable, and so is the reading behind each choice.

reviewPrompt: This week, watch the hand of each man who approaches to greet you, and match what he offers before adding anything of your own.
